text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Bonn and Paris want to counteract differences creeping into their relations.
- German Farmers' Association (DBV) defends the large subsidies the agricultural sector receives.
- German police accuses Amnesty International of not telling the truth about police treatment of suspects. Officers say they are considering taking legal action against Amnesty.
- Government plans to have signifcantly more borrowing than new investment in 1997 supplementary budget and 1998 budget.
- German industrial orders fell by 0.8 percent in May from the previous month.
HANDELSBLATT
- Disgraced tycoon Juergen Schneider accuses big banks of share of responsibility for collapse of his real estate empire.
- Banks free to set their own charges for customers from other banks who use their cash machines.
- Lufthansa close to agreement on tourist industry tie-up with retailer Karstadt.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- State premiers reject government plan for apprentices to spend more time in the workplace and less at vocational training collges.

- Gerhard Schroeder, the opposition Social Democrats' chief negotiator on energy policy, declares talks with the government on joint legislation cannot continue now Bonn has decided to present its own bill.
- Schnieder admits "manipulation" in presenting applications for loans and predictions of income from rent.
- Ifo institute expects companies to invest four percent more in west German industry this year, compared with 1996.
DIE WELT
- Police hold protest in Bonn against plans for cuts in public spending which would cut their pay.
- Ruling coalition agrees basic details of 1997 supplementary budget and 1998 budget.
- 1996 was a good year for big German companies, annual Welt survey shows.
